h1: Who to call first when a licence renewal is delayed
title: When a Brewery Licence Renewal Stalls | Craft Beer School
desc: A brewery licence renewal is late and expiry is close. Who to call first, what to ask and how to protect trading and cash while you wait.
teaser: A renewal stuck in a queue can close a taproom. The order you make the calls in matters more than how many you make.
standfirst: Every Indian brewery renews its licences every year. Every few years one gets stuck. When expiry is a week away and the status still reads pending, panic makes the wrong calls. Here is the order we would work through.
sections: First, find out exactly where it is stuck

Before you call anyone senior, get the facts. Open the online portal, if your state has one. Note the application number, the date submitted and the current status. Then call the dealing officer or the office that processes it and ask three questions: has the file reached the right desk, is anything missing and is there a query pending?

In our experience, most delays are a missing document, an unpaid fee or a query letter that went to an old email address. Those can be fixed in a day. A delay with no reason given is rarer. It needs a different approach.

If you use a licensing consultant, call them next, with the facts in hand. A good consultant knows how the local office works, which forms trip people up and how to raise a query correctly. If you do not use one, this is the moment to find one. A few days of fees costs far less than a week of closed taps.

Ask the consultant one direct question: can we keep trading while the renewal is pending? In some states, a renewal applied for in time with fees paid lets you continue. In others it does not. Rules vary by state and change, so get the answer in writing, not as a phone reassurance.
Third, tell your landlord, bank and key suppliers

If there is any chance you will have to stop selling, tell the people whose money depends on you before they hear it elsewhere. A landlord who learns about a closure from a customer is less patient than one who got a call. A bank with a working capital line wants to hear about cash risk early.

Work out the number first. If the taproom takes ₹80,000 on an average day and fixed costs run at ₹40,000 a day, every closed day burns ₹40,000 of cash with nothing coming in. Ten days is ₹4 lakh. That figure shapes every other conversation, including whether to pay for faster help. Our guide to first year cash flow covers the buffer you want for exactly this.
Fourth, prepare the team and the beer

Brief the taproom manager and head brewer quietly. Slow or pause new brews if a closure is likely, because beer sitting in a full fermenter you cannot sell costs money and quality. A pale ale held cold for an extra two weeks is fine. A hazy IPA held warm loses its hop aroma quickly.

Keep staff informed without spreading alarm. People hear rumours fast in a small brewery. A short, honest briefing keeps your best people from answering a recruiter's call that week.
What not to do while you wait

Do not keep selling on an expired licence because someone said it would be fine. Do not pay anyone to speed things up. Do not argue with the officer handling your file. Do not take to social media about the delay. Each of these can turn a slow renewal into a refused one.

Keep a dated log of every call, email and visit: who you spoke to and what they said. If the delay drags, that log is what your consultant or lawyer will want first.
Know which licence is actually late

A brewery in India runs on several approvals at once. Not all of them stop trade if they lapse. An excise licence that expires usually means no sales until it is renewed. A delayed signage permission or trade licence renewal is a problem, but rarely one that closes the taps that same evening. Your FSSAI licence sits somewhere in between, because the kitchen and the beer both depend on it.

Rank your licences by what happens the day after expiry. Sort them into three groups: those that stop beer sales, those that stop food and those that bring a fine or notice but let you trade. Put most of your energy on the first group. A founder chasing a signage renewal while the excise file sits unopened has the order wrong.

Ask your consultant to confirm the list for your state, because the answer varies by state and changes over time. Keep the ranked list at the front of your licence file so whoever is in charge knows which delay is an emergency.

After the renewal comes through, fix the system so it does not happen again. Put every licence in one calendar with three reminders: 90, 60 and 30 days before expiry. Start renewals at the 90 day mark. Keep scanned copies of every document the last renewal needed, so the next one starts with a complete file.

A delayed renewal is a cash flow problem, a staffing problem and a compliance problem at once. Planning for all three before it happens is what separates breweries that wobble from ones that close.

Your first step: open your calendar now and add a 90 day reminder for every licence you hold.
faqs: Can a brewery keep trading while its licence renewal is pending?
It depends on the state and on whether you applied in time with fees paid. Ask your licensing consultant and get the answer in writing before relying on it.
What usually causes a licence renewal delay?
Most delays come from a missing document, an unpaid fee or a query that never reached the applicant. Checking the portal and calling the dealing office usually finds it.
When should I start a brewery licence renewal?
Start about 90 days before expiry, with reminders at 60 and 30 days, so a delay never reaches the last week.
